title: Masked Position Modeling as a Pre-Training Strategy for Foundational Deformable Image Registration Models.
source: PubMed · IEEE transactions on medical imaging
desc: [IEEE transactions on medical imaging] The core objective of deformable image registration (DIR), estimating a displacement vector field that aligns two images, is fundamentally the same across imaging modalities and anatomical regions. Although this shared objective should imply the use of foundation models, most deep learning approaches for DIR operate within narrow domain-specific settings. Vision Transformers (ViTs) are the predominant choice for foundation models in many image processing tasks due to their excellent generalization capabilities and robustness to domain shifts. However, their use remains largely underexplored for DIR, which we attribute to a lack of suitable pre-training schemes. To address this need, we introduce MPM-Reg, a transferable, modality-agnostic training paradigm based on masked position modeling (MPM), enabling the use of fully transformer-based models as foundation models for image registration. Unlike conventional masked data modeling, which predicts the content of masked image patches, MPM masks the positional information and predicts the spatial relationship between image patches. Initially, we employ MPM on single images, which naturally aligns self-supervised pre-training of ViTs with the downstream registration task. Subsequently, we extend MPM to predict the positions of target patches within source images, re-formulating DIR through the lens of MPM. Experiments across eleven diverse datasets demonstrate MPM-Reg's competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Crucially, MPM-Reg benefits from heterogeneous multi-domain data, which degrades the performance of existing methods, paving the way for scalable foundation models for DIR.

title: Multicentre benchmark of PSMA PET/CT and mpMRI fusion for non-invasive clinically significant prostate cancer diagnosis
desc: Clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) guides-biopsy and treatment decisions, yet its non-invasive diagnosis remains challenging. The incremental value of PSMA PET/CT beyond multiparametric MRI (mpMRI), and the optimal strategy for multimodal fusion, remain unclear. We established a real-world, multicentre benchmark using 527 patients from three hospitals with fully paired PSMA PET, CT, T2-weighted MRI, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), together with pathology-confirmed biopsy labels. Models were developed in one centre ( n = 363) and independently evaluated in two external centres ( n = 164). We compared frozen pretrained encoders, fine-tuned 2D and 3D CNN and Vision Transformer models, three fusion strategies, and an interpretable cross-modal Transformer. PSMA PET provided the greatest incremental value, with its removal producing the largest AUC reduction internally (−0.077) and externally (−0.055), supported by the highest attention attribution (αPET = 0.45). PSMA PET/CT also outperformed mpMRI externally (AUC 0.753 vs. 0.653). DWI was the principal source of domain shift, as its exclusion improved external AUC by 0.079 amid inter-centre b-value heterogeneity. Intermediate fusion performed most consistently internally, whereas late fusion and pretrained 2D models generalised better externally. This benchmark supports robust, non-invasive csPCa diagnosis by identifying modalities and fusion strategies that generalise reliably across institutions.

title: Artificial intelligence in hepatitis: Advances in diagnosis, treatment optimization, and prognostic prediction.
source: PubMed · The Journal of international medical research
desc: [The Journal of international medical research] Hepatitis remains a major global health challenge and an important contributor to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality worldwide. Early diagnosis, effective treatment selection, and accurate prognostic stratification remain critical unmet needs in clinical hepatology. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a promising approach to addressing these challenges through the integration and analysis of large-scale, heterogeneous biomedical datasets. This narrative review synthesizes advances in artificial intelligence applications in hepatitis research and clinical practice published over the past decade, organized across three clinical domains: diagnosis, treatment optimization, and prognosis prediction. In the diagnostic domain, artificial intelligence-based approaches have been applied to medical imaging, digital pathology, and multi-omics data to enhance the detection, classification, and staging of liver disease. In the therapeutic domain, machine learning models have been increasingly deployed to support drug discovery, optimize therapeutic regimens, and predict individual treatment responses. In the prognostic domain, artificial intelligence-driven models have shown promising performance in predicting disease progression, survival outcomes, and clinical complications. Nevertheless, key limitations persist, including data heterogeneity, limited external generalizability, and barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will depend on prospective multicenter evaluation, use of interoperable multimodal data, development of transparent models that account for uncertainty, and evidence that artificial intelligence improves clinical decisions and patient outcomes rather than performance metrics alone.

title: Clinical Application of Artificial Intelligence Methods in Diagnostic Imaging of Pulmonary Nodules
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Shanghai East Hospital; conditions: Pulmonary Nodules, Lung Neoplasms, Lung Diseases; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 10000; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] This is a retrospective, multicenter observational study evaluating the clinical value of combining high-resolution (1024×1024 matrix) targeted CT scans with an artificial intelligence (AI) deep learning system to distinguish between benign and malignant pulmonary nodules. By analyzing existing medical records and CT images of adult patients (aged 18 and older) with pulmonary nodules (3-30 mm) who have confirmed diagnoses (via postoperative pathology）, this study aims to assess the diagnostic accuracy and efficiency of the AI system. The study plans to enroll approximately 10,000 cases from three hospitals in Shanghai. The primary goal is to evaluate the AI system's diagnostic performance (such as sensitivity, specificity, and Area Under the ROC Curve) and compare it with the performance of radiologists, ultimately exploring whether this combined approach can provide more accurate clinical diagnoses and reduce unnecessary procedures.

title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
desc: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.

title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents
desc: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

title: Mathematical AI Predicts 40% and 57% Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness Against H1N1 and H3N2, Respectively, for the 2026--2027 U.S. Season
desc: Background: Clinical influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) has often been low over the past two decades, highlighting the need for preseason VE forecasting. Timely forecasts could help health authorities plan prevention strategies and allocate healthcare resources. However, preseason forecasting of clinical influenza VE remains relatively uncommon. Methods: We obtained hemagglutinin (HA) sequences from GISAID for U.S. specimens collected in August--September before each influenza season from 2010--2011 through 2024--2025. After quality screening, we compared each virus with the corresponding vaccine target strain for the same season and subtype or lineage using two mathematical distances based on amino acid patterns in the HA protein. We calculated mean distances for each season and subtype or lineage and paired them with published clinical VE estimates, yielding 26 observations across 13 seasons. Using a mathematical AI approach, we fitted linear regression models of VE against each distance and evaluated their predictive performance by forecasting later seasons using data from earlier seasons, with the historical mean VE for each subtype or lineage as a reference. We then applied the same approach to 87 HA sequences collected in August--September 2026 to forecast VE for the 2026--2027 season. Results: We generated component-specific forecasts of influenza VE for the upcoming 2026--2027 U.S. season. Both mathematical distances were negatively associated with historical VE, indicating that greater differences between circulating viruses and vaccine strains were associated with lower VE. The topological model forecast VE of 40.3%, 56.9%, and 47.1% against A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria, respectively, whereas the geometric model forecast corresponding VE values of 34.0%, 56.8%, and 51.1%.

title: Development and Validation of an Automated Image-Based Method for Prognostic Stratification in Lung Adenocarcinoma using Immunohistochemical Markers
desc: We present an automated image-based framework for quantifying biomarker expression in immunohistochemical (IHC) images and introduce the Marker Expression Level (MEL) score as an objective alternative to visual H-scoring. MEL addresses key limitations of existing automated methods by integrating tissue-region segmentation with tumour-area-weighted marker quantification, normalization to mitigate inter-sample and inter-batch staining variability, and robust quantification of nuclear, cytoplasmic, and membrane-associated biomarkers. The complete pipeline was developed as an open-source Fiji/ImageJ tool and is publicly available. We evaluated MEL using IHC images from 128 lung adenocarcinoma patients stained for BRCA1, GLUT1, and QKI, three markers forming a prognostic signature previously described by our group. Tissue regions were segmented using a machine learning-based Fiji plugin, and MEL scores were calculated within tumour regions. A normalization strategy accounted for inter-TMA staining variability. Agreement with visual H-scores was assessed using Spearman correlation. Prognostic performance was evaluated using Cox regression to derive a Combined Prognostic Index (CPI) incorporating MEL scores and tumour stage. Segmentation achieved high accuracy across tissue regions (Dice coefficients 0.69-0.99), with lower performance in highly immune-infiltrated stromal areas. MEL scores significantly correlated with visual H-scores for all markers ({rho} = 0.61-0.69, p < 0.001). Normalization improved agreement for GLUT1 ({rho} = 0.39 to 0.62). The derived CPI stratified patients into distinct risk groups with significant differences in disease-free and overall survival (p < 0.05), comparable to visual scoring. MEL provides a reproducible and scalable alternative to expert visual H-scoring and standard semi-automated approaches such as QuPath. Its integration with prognostic modelling reproduced a validated survival signature with performance comparable to expert scoring, supporting clinical and translational applicability. MEL is not a marginal refinement of existing digital scoring methods, but rather a clinically oriented and biologically adaptable framework designed to improve the robustness and reproducibility of automated IHC quantification.

title: Systemwide adoption patterns of ambient AI scribe technology in an integrated academic health system
desc: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes may reduce documentation burden, but little is known about their adoption during enterprise-scale ambulatory rollout. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 2901 ambulatory clinicians at an integrated academic health system using linked electronic health record and vendor usage data from December 2024 through May 2025. Clinician adoption was defined as any use during the study period, and monthly visit-level uptake as the proportion of eligible ambulatory visits in which the ambient AI scribe was used. Adoption and uptake varied substantially across practice settings, specialties, and clinician types. Clinician-level adoption was highest in community internal medicine (67%), community general pediatrics (69%), and academic neurology (53%), and lowest in academic general surgery (16%), obstetrics and gynecology (18%), and psychiatry (19%). Community attending physicians and advanced practice providers showed marked increases in median visit-level uptake, reaching approximately 80%-90% in some groups by May 2025. Distinct longitudinal patterns included slow and steady adoption, early use followed by discontinuation, transient use, and late adoption. These findings suggest that implementation support and evaluation strategies should be tailored to local practice context rather than applied uniformly across a health system.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Parasitology: A holistic perspective from diagnosis to therapeutics.
desc: [Experimental parasitology] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated to address challenges in parasite detection, disease surveillance, and therapeutic development. This narrative review examines current and emerging AI applications in parasitology across diagnostics, drug discovery, genomics, epidemiology, education, and public health decision-making, with particular emphasis on diagnostic applications. Machine learning and deep learning methods support automated parasite detection, classification, and quantification in microscopic images, alongside medical image analysis and arthropod identification. Applications are discussed for malaria, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, cystic echinococcosis, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and intestinal protozoal infections. Beyond diagnosis, AI-assisted approaches support compound screening, drug repurposing, toxicity prediction, and prioritization of potential therapeutic targets. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses also offer opportunities to investigate parasite biology and predict drug resistance. Surveillance models may inform outbreak forecasting and targeted control, although their operational value requires evaluation in the intended settings. Educational applications remain emerging, and the benefits of digital learning should be distinguished from those attributable specifically to AI. Across these domains, performance on curated datasets does not establish clinical utility or generalizability. Major barriers include limited representative datasets, insufficient external and prospective validation, infrastructure constraints, and concerns regarding privacy, bias, and accountability. Future progress requires reproducible evaluation, experimental validation of therapeutic candidates, and assessment of clinical and public health benefits. AI is therefore best positioned as a complementary tool that supports parasitological expertise, with responsible implementation guided by transparency, equitable access, and human oversight.

title: Longitudinal AI-Assisted Management of Indeterminate Pulmonary Nodules
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology; conditions: Pulmonary Nodules, Lung Neoplasms; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 6000; status: RECRUITING] Patients with indeterminate lung nodules often face a choice between continued CT surveillance and invasive investigation. This trial compares management with or without access to an AI report that matches nodules across real serial CT scans, measures change, and estimates validated malignancy or invasiveness risks. The principal question is whether offering the report reduces lung resections that yield benign pathology over 24 months. Diagnostic delay, cancer stage, treatment opportunity, complications, and longer-term cancer outcomes are also assessed.

title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
desc: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

title: Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival Inference for EHR Association Studies With Limited Chart Review
desc: Objective: To reduce bias and improve precision in survival association studies using electronic health record (EHR) data when computational phenotypes (CPs) for outcomes and covariates are error-prone and chart review is limited. Materials and Methods: We developed Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival (MAPS) regression, which combines chart-reviewed and CP-derived labels across different validation patterns. MAPS uses a discrete-time survival model with a complementary log-log link to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). It incorporates data-adaptive augmentation weights, inverse-probability sampling weights, and patient-level cluster-robust variance estimation. We compared MAPS with chart-reviewed data (CRD) and CP-only analyses in simulation studies and a masked-validation study of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) among 1,026 patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Results: In the main simulations, MAPS produced approximately unbiased estimates and generally near-nominal 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, with narrower intervals than CRD. CP-only estimates became increasingly biased as CP errors increased. In the EHR analysis, MAPS estimates closely agreed with fully validated estimates and improved precision over CRD, particularly at lower validation rates. CP-only analysis suggested increased irAE risk associated with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID; HR=1.53; 95% CI, 1.12-2.09), whereas the fully validated analysis did not (HR=0.93; 95% CI, 0.67-1.29). Discussion: Precision gains depended on CP quality and validation rates, while small validation samples may affect confidence interval coverage. Conclusion: MAPS provides a flexible and efficient approach to EHR-based survival inference by combining limited chart-reviewed data with error-prone CPs across different validation patterns.

title: AlphaGenome informed machine learning for pathogenicity prediction of germline mutations
desc: Accurate interpretation of germline variants remains a central challenge in clinical genomics. Existing in silico pathogenicity predictors often provide incomplete coverage or restricted to missense variants from the coding region, leaving the variants from splice sites, -UTR, and intronic regions under-scored. We present AGVarPred, a gradient-boosted classifier designed to predict the pathogenicity of germline mutants, with a broad consequence-class coverage across SNVs and indels. Here, the population allele frequency from gnomAD, functional consequence annotations from Ensembl VEP, and cell-type-specific functional genomic scores from the AlphaGenome platform were integrated to develop the classifier. Using a gene-level split of 134,002 high-confidence ClinVar variants across 9,222 genes, AGVarPred achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9753 (95% CI 0.9731-0.9775) and a AUC-PR of 0.9606 on 12,385 scored internal test variants. A paired DeLong analysis showed that the full model significantly outperformed an allele-frequency-plus-VEP model ({Delta}AUC = 0.1539, 95% CI 0.1489-0.1589; p < 1 x 10-300), supporting a substantial incremental contribution from AlphaGenome-derived features. Performance remained strong when restricted to SNVs (AUC-ROC 0.9558) and was also high for indels (AUC-ROC 0.9532). On five external benchmarks, AUC-ROCs ranged from 0.528 on a functional-assay-derived benchmark to 0.977 on a clinically curated deafness database, reflecting its dependence on benchmark composition and label source. A separate analysis of the VIP Database, whose pathogenic labels are ClinVar-derived, showed consistent performance (AUC-ROC of 0.892) in held-out genes. AGVarPred scored 100% of evaluated variants in the external benchmarks, whereas AlphaMissense and REVEL covered only small fractions of non-missense variants. Model interpretation indicated that gnomAD allele frequency was the dominant individual predictor; the 111 AlphaGenome features provided complementary functional signal, with splicing and chromatin assays contributing to the largest share of the AlphaGenome SHAP mass. A web-based interface for AGVarPred is available at https://pankaj357.github.io/AGVarPred/ to facilitate the submission of normalized GRCh38 germline variants and retrieval of pathogenicity predictions using the frozen AGVarPred model.

title: Exhaustive white blood cell extraction and profiling across whole-slide images of blood and bone marrow smears
desc: Blood and bone marrow smears are central to diagnosing hematological disorders. While whole-slide scanning enables automated single-cell profiling at scale, the computational burden of gigapixel images has confined automated analysis to manually pre-selected regions of interest. Here, we present HemAutomaton, a framework built on neural cellular automata that extracts white blood cells across entire whole-slide images without manual region selection and with minimal annotation requirements. HemAutomaton matches the in-domain detection accuracy of Faster R-CNN while surpassing it under domain shifts, operating at a fraction of the computational cost and with over 10,000-fold fewer parameters. Across three blood cancer cohorts, we extract over 100 million single-cell images and achieve annotation-efficient differential counting via few-shot classification using a pretrained hematology foundation model. Slide-wide spatial analysis uncovers consistent blast-frequency gradients across smears and demonstrates that automated blast counts match expert evaluations within inter-expert variability. Scaling automated profiling from hundreds to tens of thousands of cells per smear overcomes conventional sampling limits and establishes the foundation for more sensitive AI supported hematological assessments.

title: GliaDose: An alternative approach for clinical CAR-T dose prediction via PBPK–glioblastoma-on-a-chip integration
desc: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor with poor prognosis and limited treatment options. Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapy for GBM. However, unlike conventional drugs, CAR-T cells are living therapeutics that exhibit non-linear pharmacokinetics, expansion, and complex tissue trafficking, making conventional animal-to-human dose extrapolation unreliable. Furthermore, species-specific differences and the vasculature limit the translational relevance of preclinical models. To address these challenges, we developed GliaDose, a hybrid framework that integrates physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling with a vascularized glioblastoma-on-a-chip (GoC) platform to support quantitative first-in-human dose (FIHD) prediction for CAR-T therapy. The PBPK model was parameterized exclusively with human physiological data and incorporates a brain-tumor compartment to explicitly capture CAR-T transport across the vasculature. Complementarily, the GoC platform recapitulates key features of the GBM microenvironment, including three-dimensional tumor architecture, extracellular matrix, and perfusable human vascular networks, enabling assessment of CAR-T transmigration under flow conditions. Integration of GoC-derived efficacy data into the PBPK framework enabled quantitative dose–response predictions and identified vascular barriers as critical determinants of CAR-T tumor access. GliaDose provides a human-relevant, mechanistic alternative to animal-based dose selection and may improve FIHD prediction and personalized CAR-T therapy for GBM.

title: Bottlenecks in cardiovascular prevention: Can artificial intelligence close the gap?
desc: [Archives of cardiovascular diseases] Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in France, despite current preventive strategies and evidence-based therapies. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach to overcoming several of these barriers, with the potential to improve cardiovascular prevention across the entire spectrum of care. Upstream, AI can enhance risk stratification through the integration of clinical, biological, imaging, environmental, behavioural and longitudinal data, thereby moving cardiovascular prevention toward an AI-augmented precision medicine paradigm, in which risk assessments are increasingly individualized. Downstream, AI-enabled clinical decision support systems may improve guideline implementation, reduce therapeutic inertia and support individualized treatment optimization. Generative AI may also strengthen patient education, personalize risk communication, promote healthy behaviours and improve long-term adherence through adaptive coaching and continuous monitoring. However, translating these promises into meaningful improvements in cardiovascular outcomes will require overcoming substantial technological, organizational, regulatory and societal challenges. These challenges include ensuring data quality and information system interoperability, addressing inequalities in access to digital health technologies, improving the acceptability of AI among patients and healthcare professionals through rigorous evaluation and, critically, adapting healthcare systems to absorb, triage and manage the potentially large number of at-risk individuals identified by AI-enabled prevention strategies. By examining these barriers, this review highlights that AI mainly shifts the bottlenecks of prevention downstream, rather than removing them, and outlines the conditions required for AI, beyond intrinsic performance, to improve cardiovascular prevention in routine clinical practice.

title: Predicting the Optimal Empirical Antibiotic Therapy for Bacteremia Using an Artificial Intelligence-based Model
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Nantes University Hospital; conditions: Bacteremia; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 8765; status: COMPLETED] Bacteremia, a common infection associated with high morbidity and mortality, requires prompt and appropriate antibiotic treatment. Numerous studies have shown that the appropriate use of antibiotics helps improve the prognosis of patients, reduce the selection of pathogenic organisms, the emergence of antibiotic resistance, adverse treatment effects, and healthcare costs. The Nantes University Hospital Center has operated a Biomedical Data Warehouse (BDW) since 2018. The growing availability of data through BDWs thus enables the development of decision-support tools based on machine learning. The primary objective of the OPTIBact project is to predict the optimal empirical antibiotic for hospitalized patients with bacteremia using a machine learning-based predictive model using data from the Nantes University Hospital's BDW. As secondary objectives, the study aims: * To compare the performance of the predictive model for the optimal empirical antibiotic against standard patient care * To estimate the expected benefit of the predictive model compared to real-world practice in terms of clinical outcomes * To predict the optimal dosage of empirical antibiotic therapy * To compare the performance of the predictive model for optimal empirical antibiotic therapy dosing with standard patient care * To describe inpatient patients in Nantes University Hospital who received optimal antibiotic therapy and those who did not * To Identify predictors of antibiotic resistance in bacteria isolated from blood cultures, stratified by pathogen type.

title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery
desc: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.

title: The Patient Is Always Right? Evaluating Sycophancy in Medical Diagnosis with Graded Patient Beliefs
desc: More people are seeking out general-purpose AI models for medical advice, including diagnosis. Yet, AI models are susceptible to sycophancy, like validating users' beliefs even when they are untrue, which could lead to false positive diagnoses. Here, we evaluate how nine AI models change their diagnostic decision when a patient presents a belief that they have a specific (but incorrect) medical condition. We vary how close the user belief is to the clinical evidence presented. Models sycophantically adopt the patient's belief on average 23.2\% of the time---sometimes even when the patient proposes a fictional, made-up condition. We also varied different personas, including a Rare Disease Claimer that got models to accept their belief 43.0\% of the time. Additional analyses find that medical fine-tuning and model scale makes models less susceptible to changing their diagnoses. Sycophantic bias in medical diagnosis raises implications for safety, especially as more people are using AI for health support.

title: A Pipeline for Predicting Variant Associations with Complex Disorders via Functional Annotations
desc: The study of complex disorders is limited by the lack of structured data sets that integrate genetic association signals with rich functional annotations. While genome wide association studies (GWAS) provide large collections of associated variants, these are heterogeneous, studydependent, and not directly suitable for machine learning applications. Although frameworks such as Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) offer comprehensive variant-level features, there is no standardised procedure to construct curated, balanced, and reproducible data sets for the systematic study of complex traits. We introduce a scalable and reproducible pipeline for generating CADD-annotated variant data sets associated with complex disorders defined via Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO) terms. The pipeline integrates GWAS summary statistics, genome mapping, chromosomestratified negative sampling, and large-scale annotation, while addressing class imbalance and feature redundancy. The resulting data sets provide curated, balanced, and annotation-rich representations of variant-trait associations, suitable for statistical learning, systematic model evaluation and comparison, and analysis of functional annotation contributions and interactions.

title: Population-scale machine learning models to estimate individual-level risk for acute respiratory infection
desc: Background: Models based on administrative population health records can help improve understanding of disease and hospitalisation risk. This understanding can support evidence-based population health policy and processes. Influenza and other acute respiratory diseases place a large, inequitable burden on the New Zealand population and health care resources. We have developed and evaluated models using retrospective New Zealand hospitalisation records linked to other administrative data. Methods: We analysed linked annual records for approximately 4.85 - 5.36 million people in 2017 - 2024. For each year, models were trained to distinguish people who experienced at least one hospitalisation associated with respiratory infectious disease from those without such a hospitalisation during that year. Six algorithms and eight variable sets were assessed using five-fold cross-validation grouped by demographic profile. Variables comprised demographics, continuous hospital-based (M3) and pharmaceutical-based (P3) morbidity indices, and influenza vaccination status. Models trained on one year were also evaluated on data from the following year. Performance measures were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the average precision score (APS). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) described model contributions, including paired vaccination-input changes in 2024. Findings: Annual national hospitalisation prevalence ranged from 1.01% to 1.60%. With all variables, mean cross-validation AUROC and APS were 0.8430 and 0.1283 for LightGBM (LGB), and 0.8415 and 0.1285 for XGBoost (XGB). Adding both morbidity indices to the demographics increased LGB APS from 0.0720 to 0.1158; adding vaccination further increased it to 0.1283. Next-year AUROC and APS averaged 0.8429 and 0.1267 for LGB and 0.8423 and 0.1277 for XGB. Age and morbidity were the most influential variables. Among vaccinated individuals, SHAP analysis indicated that vaccination contributed most strongly towards lower model-estimated hospitalisation risk in the oldest age group. Interpretation: Combining historical morbidity and vaccination information in gradient boosting models improved the ability to distinguish between people who experienced respiratory hospitalisation and those who did not in annual New Zealand population data. title: Visual-affective decoding enhances neurofunctional objective and generalizable signatures in unseen adolescent depression diagnosis
desc: Adolescent major depressive disorder is a highly prevalent and debilitating condition, yet objective and generalizable neurofunctional signatures remain elusive. Existing neuroimaging approaches largely rely on resting-state fMRI, or controlled tasks often lack ecological validity and generalizable signatures of depression-related neural dysfunctions. This study proposes a Visual–Affective Decoding (VAD) framework integrating cross-subject visual and affective decoding from whole-brain fMRI acquired during naturalistic movie viewing. A dual-pathway anomaly detection model trained exclusively on healthy controls establishes normative brain function and identifies MDD through deviations from this norm. In 200 adolescents (112 MDD, 88 HC), VAD achieved an AUC of 0.87, 95.56% sensitivity, 83.89% accuracy, and 72.22% specificity. Using the same anomaly threshold, it generalized to an independent external adolescent cohort (70 MDD, 68 HC), achieving an AUC of 0.81 with an accuracy of 75.36%, supporting its cross-site generalizability. VAD further revealed interpretable neurofunctional signatures, including blunted emotional reactivity, attenuated visual representation, and affective patterns consistent with emotional rumination. Region-level contribution analyses identified dissociable visual- and affective-sensitive cortical regions, consistent with dysfunctions in visual, default-mode, salience, and higher-order associative networks. These findings demonstrate that VAD provides objective, interpretable, and generalizable neurofunctional signatures for adolescent depression diagnosis and clinically relevant biomarker development.

title: AI-Guided Histopathological and Molecular Phenotyping of Salivary Glands in Sjögren's Disease: Subtyping, Mechanistic Insights, and Translational Implications-A Systematic Review and Structured Functional Synthesis.
desc: [Medical sciences (Basel, Switzerland)] Salivary-gland biopsy is central to Sjögren's disease (SjD) assessment, but conventional measures incompletely capture glandular heterogeneity. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) applications to SjD salivary-gland histopathology and molecular profiling, including biological and translational validation. PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched. Eligible studies used salivary-gland tissue as the primary analytical substrate or provided substantive glandular validation of systemic AI/ML findings. Evidence was synthesized functionally because of methodological heterogeneity. Twenty-five studies were included. AI/ML identified histopathological and molecular phenotypes spanning immune/interferon activation, tissue architecture and immune-cell organization, epithelial stress and metabolic/cell-death remodeling, and translational response. Only a limited subset progressed beyond computational or tissue-level confirmation to functional perturbation, pharmacological testing, in vivo validation, or human treatment-response assessment. Recurrent public-dataset reuse, small cohorts, heterogeneous pipelines, and limited independent validation constrained reproducibility. AI/ML supports multidimensional SjD glandular phenotyping and shows emerging translational potential, but demonstrated clinical or therapeutic utility remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter validation is required before AI-derived glandular phenotypes can inform routine patient stratification or therapeutic decision-making.

Clinicians review the report alongside images and clinical evidence and retain responsibility for testing and treatment. The trial asks whether AI-assisted care reduces death or new invasive respiratory or circulatory support within 28 days. Patients are followed after discharge through day 90.

title: WORTH Benchmark: Evidence Discovery under Not-Fully-Cooperative Information -- A Two-Episode Pilot
desc: Existing reasoning evaluations typically provide task-relevant information to models as available premises, rarely examining concurrently how models discover evidence autonomously and how information presentation within narratives guides or obscures judgment. This paper proposes the WORTH Benchmark: models read original mystery narratives without clue annotations, autonomously select key clue sentences, identify case participants, and explain their reasoning process. The narrative materials are designed by professional authors such that evidence facilitating reasoning coexists with narrative arrangements that delay the revelation of truth. We report a pilot experiment under full-story conditions across two episodes, conducting a total of 70 formal runs on models, of which 67 runs are content-scorable. Scoring separately records hits on author-designated key clue sentences and participant selections; natural language explanations are used for case diagnosis and are not scored independently. The results show that clue hits and participant judgments are not synchronized; across 37 content-scorable runs in Episode 02, 31 runs simultaneously selected the same set of incorrect participants, while adjacent suspicion-oriented and exoneration-oriented sentences were selected 25 times and 0 times, respectively. These phenomena illustrate the diagnostic value of component-wise analysis and suggest that not-fully-cooperative informational relationships may influence evidence selection and judgment. This study only implements full-story conditions for two episodes, and does not establish stable model rankings or infer general mechanisms on this basis; human player records have not yet been cleaned, and this version does not report human-model comparisons.

title: Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis
desc: Augmented large language model (LLM) systems have reported high benchmark accuracies in rare disease diagnosis, yet their real-world clinical utility remains unproven. A recent meta-analysis flagged augmented LLM diagnostic evaluations as having a high risk of bias due to suspected data leakage; however, the precise impact of these vulnerabilities on model inference has yet to be fully quantified. In this study, we present a comprehensive empirical audit to quantify evaluation artifacts across prevailing AI paradigms, using a repository of over 60,000 cases from diverse public and independent clinical cohorts. By reconstructing a state-of-the-art agentic framework, we demonstrate that candidate-space contamination artificially inflates performance: enforcing strict cross-dataset isolation resulted in a marked performance decline, with the cross-dataset mean Recall@1 decreasing from 54.3% (under conventional one-vs-rest evaluation) to 40.3% (Hedges' g = 0.94). Similar spatial overfitting in supervised classifiers caused diagnostic accuracy to drop from an internal mean of 42.9% to 16.7% across external cohorts (Cohen's d = 2.01). Furthermore, we quantify how LLMs infer diagnoses by exploiting retrospective therapeutic cues in clinical narratives, and how temporal misalignment in foundational knowledge bases leads to performance fluctuations. We conclude that prevailing evaluation protocols for augmented LLM systems inadvertently reflect data leakage rather than genuine medical reasoning. To address these systematic artifacts, we propose a rigorous evaluation framework - coupling strict data-isolation protocols with standardized benchmarking safeguards - to ensure future diagnostic AI for rare diseases is evaluated on actual clinical robustness.

title: flodl-bio: First Rust data, transformers and model layer for entire deep learning on biological sequences
desc: Python ecosystem dominates the deep learning framework. flodl-bio is a Rust crate that extends flodl, a libtorch-backed deep-learning framework, with deep learning on biological sequences. To our knowledge, flodl-bio is the first Rust crate that provides a comprehensive and practical deep learning for the biological applications, which includes the alphabet-aware sequence encoding, including one-hot and k-mer representations, padded sequences, and channels-first batches. It also includes several FASTA parsing and graph construction utilities for adjacency matrices, GCN-normalised adjacency matrices, graph Laplacians, residue contact maps, and de Bruijn graphs. Among the added functionalities, it includes AUROC and AUPRC with their associated curves; classification metrics, and the export of learned convolutional filters as MEME motifs and seeded splits. Deep biological learning includes a multi-width motif CNN, a dilated residual CNN, bidirectional LSTM and GRU architectures, and transformer encoder. On the five human transcription-factor-binding datasets in the GUE benchmark, a motif CNN with approximately 10,000 parameters, trained from scratch, outperforms all published CNN baselines. It also superseded the 2.5-billion-parameter Nucleotide Transformer on two datasets and DNABERT-2 on one. Given a fixed hardware configuration and software stack, experiments are reproducible at the bit level. See Supplementary Table S2 of Supplementary Material. flodl-bio is written in Rust and released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/sablokg/flodl-bio. The core builds with stable Rust and has no dependencies. The model tier is enabled with the flodl Cargo feature (cuda for NVIDIA GPUs) and requires libtorch and Rust 1.91 or later. The evaluation harness is in the repository's experiments directory, and the complete run outputs are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23321850

title: AI-Assisted Writing Across Medical Journals: Heterogeneity in Prevalence and Trends
desc: Background: Estimates of generative artificial intelligence (AI) use in the medical literature vary widely, potentially reflecting differences across journals. We estimated changes in the prevalence of AI-generated writing over time using abstracts from 12 general medical journals. Methods: We randomly sampled up to 200 abstracts per journal-year from publications dated January 1, 2020, through August 8, 2026. Abstracts were scored using GPTZero, with journal-specific thresholds calibrated to fix a 1% false-positive rate (FPR) in the pre-AI baseline period (2020-2021). We estimated annual detector-positive proportions and calculated a publication-volume-weighted estimate across sampled journals. Associations with journal impact factor, publication model, and publication volume were examined descriptively. Results: Among 15,268 abstracts, estimated prevalence of AI-generated text increased after 2022, with substantial variation in timing and magnitude across journals. In 2026 through August 8, prevalence estimates ranged from 5.7% (95% CI, 2.1%-10.0%) in the New England Journal of Medicine to 83.5% (95% CI, 77.1%-87.5%) in Frontiers in Medicine. The publication-volume-weighted estimate across sampled journals was 66.7% (95% CI, 64.0%-69.2%), and trends were insensitive to specification of false-positive rate in baseline data. The proportion of abstracts showing signs of AI-generated text was lower in journals with higher impact factors and higher in fully open-access journals. Conclusions: Estimated prevalence of AI-generated text increased substantially across all sampled medical journals, with marked between-journal differences associated with journal impact factor and publication model. These findings support development of standardized, transparent AI reporting in medical publishing.

title: Clinical applications of remote patient monitoring.
source: PubMed · Current problems in pediatric and adolescent health care
desc: [Current problems in pediatric and adolescent health care] Remote patient monitoring (RPM) utilizes a variety of technologies that enable rapid transmission of health data, allowing healthcare providers to manage medical conditions outside the hospital setting. As an increasingly important component of pediatric telehealth and healthcare delivery, RPM has been successfully implemented across multiple specialties. This review highlights RPM programs at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), including initiatives in cardiology, neonatology, primary care, gastrostomy tube care, and neurology. These programs have demonstrated success in reducing unnecessary hospitalizations and emergency department visits, increasing access to care and subspecialty follow-up, and lowering mortality among children with chronic diseases. The review also examines the digital health technologies that support these programs. In addition, artificial intelligence is playing an expanding role in RPM through predictive alerts, risk stratification, and agentic monitoring tools that enable more personalized and proactive care. Despite these benefits, important challenges remain, including disparities in digital literacy, language barriers, and licensing restrictions. We propose that a hybrid care model integrating RPM, digital health technologies, and in-person visits provides a comprehensive framework for pediatric healthcare delivery. As RPM continues to expand across pediatric subspecialties, the development of telehealth "neighborhoods" may help strengthen medical homes for children with complex chronic conditions. Such models have the potential to improve clinical outcomes, enhance care coordination, and reduce healthcare disparities among vulnerable pediatric populations.

title: Comparing an AI-driven Hearing Test With the Standard Hearing Test in Adults With Hearing Loss and Tinnitus
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University College, London; conditions: Sensorineural Hearing Loss, Tinnitus; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 84; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] Background and study aims Hearing problems are becoming more common. In the UK around 18 million adults have hearing loss or hear ringing or buzzing in their ears, which is called tinnitus. Many people wait a long time to be seen, partly because there are not enough audiologists - the specialists who test hearing and treat hearing problems. The standard hearing test is called pure-tone audiometry. An audiologist plays quiet sounds at different pitches through headphones and the person presses a button each time they hear one. The test is accurate, but it takes 20 to 30 minutes to complete, and needs a trained audiologist for all of that time. For people with tinnitus and comorbidity it can be especially tiring and slow. The research team has built a version of this test that uses artificial intelligence, called AI-PTA. Instead of following a fixed pattern, it chooses each sound based on the responses already given, which should mean fewer sound presentations are needed to find the same result. The audiologist stays with the person throughout and remains in charge of the test. This study asks three questions. 1. Does AI-PTA give the same hearing results as the standard test? 2. Is it quicker? 3. And do patients and staff find it acceptable? Who can participate? Adults aged 18 or over who have been diagnosed with sensorineural hearing loss, either with or without tinnitus, and who are due to attend the Royal National ENT \& Eastman Dental Hospital in London. Participants need enough English to read and complete questionnaires and to be able to give informed consent. People who have or report hyperacusis (an unusual sensitivity to everyday sounds), an active ear infection, or recent ear surgery cannot take part. What does the study involve? People who are interested are sent information about two weeks before a hospital appointment they already have. Those who decide to take part come in about 30 minutes early, meet a research audiologist, discuss the study, and if happy to take part, sign a consent form. They fill in a short questionnaire about their hearing health. They then have two hearing tests at that visit: the standard test, which is part of their normal care, and the AI-PTA test. Half of the participants have the standard test first and half have AI-PTA first, so that the order does not affect the results. title: MedAdaptAgent: An Automatic Harness for Adapting Medical Imaging Models to New Sites
desc: Reusing pretrained medical-imaging models offers an alternative to training from scratch. A model trained for the same task may perform poorly at a new hospital because imaging protocols and preprocessing differ. Effective adaptation depends on the model architecture, domain shift, and available labels and compute. Adaptation can improve scores on a small labeled set yet reduce performance on unseen data. We present MedAdaptAgent, an automatic harness that turns a supplied model, target data, and a free-text request into a new-site adaptation workflow. Its LLM-driven Adaptation Planner uses model-site evidence to choose compatible experiments and revise subsequent adjustments. The harness requires evidence of improvement over the pretrained model, then delivers the selected model as a complete, runnable package. Evaluation spans 26 segmentation and classification transfers across architectures and compute settings, with segmentation annotation budgets ranging from zero-shot transfer to few-shot adaptation. With 20 local annotations, mean segmentation Dice rises from 0.483 to 0.774 across 10 transfers, a 60.1% relative gain, with no harmful replacements. Mean classification AUROC rises from 0.810 to 0.837 across 13 transfers, a 3.4% relative gain. Comparing adapted models with the pretrained model reduces harmful classification replacements by 30.8% versus selecting the highest-scoring model on the available labels, using identical candidates. Seven public-model deployments demonstrate adaptation and reproducible package delivery across contrast and modality shifts. A CT-to-MRI study extends the evaluation to four LLM planners, including two open-weight models. We release the code on GitHub.

title: In-silico Tandem Mass Spectral Libraries for the Blood Exposome and Metabolomics Workbench Databases: Application of Gemini Large Language Model
desc: Human body contains endogenous metabolites, nutrients and xenobiotics chemicals. These chemicals can be detected in a biospecimen using high-resolution mass spectrometry instruments, yielding metabolomic and exposomic datasets. Mass spectral libraries are critical components of these workflows to annotate experimental data with chemical information. In this data descriptor, we report mass spectral libraries for human-relevant small molecules, that are generated using Google Gemini large-language model. Using an optimized chain-of-thought prompt and instructions, we have generated mass spectra for each compound at high/medium/low energy fragmentation level. Each spectrum was reported in the NIST MSP text format for easy to use by metabolomics software. These libraries cover 91,231 unique 2D structures from the Blood Exposome Database and the Metabolomics Workbench data repository. Technical validation was shown by comparing the Gemini-generated spectra against NIST 23 mass spectral database, which demonstrated 55% accuracy. LLMs represent a useful and accessible tool for expanding in-silico spectral libraries to annotate compounds in the HRMS data for human biospecimens and may accelerate the compound annotation in metabolomics and exposomics.

title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models
desc: Physical exercise lowers blood pressure, but guidelines address broad populations and rarely consider age, comorbidities, medications or baseline severity. No structured, queryable database of exercise interventions for hypertension exists, and manual curation is not scalable. We present PAHD (Physical Activity for Hypertension Database), built with large language models (LLMs). An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records by title and abstract, then full text, selecting 255 studies. LLMs extracted each study's groups, exercise protocols, patient characteristics and results; two LLMs cross-checked the study structure, and every value carries a verbatim quote. Code standardized and joined the extractions into 17,312 records from 254 studies, one per reported comparison. Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening reached 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision, and extraction recovered 90.1% of blood pressure values with 90.5% precision. A web portal matches patients' hypertension stage and comorbidities to studies. PAHD provides a structured evidence base for personalized exercise interventions on hypertension management.

Artificial intelligence in acute stroke imaging: A comprehensive survey from imaging assessment to outcome prediction.
source: PubMed · Computerized medical imaging and graphics : the official journal of the Computerized Medical Imaging Society
desc: [Computerized medical imaging and graphics : the official journal of the Computerized Medical Imaging Society] Acute strokes encompass two main types: acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Each type involves specific imaging techniques and entails different clinical considerations. While deep learning has facilitated the analysis of stroke imaging autonomously, the technical differences between these two stroke types have not been examined within a shared analytical framework. This review addresses that gap through the examination of 84 peer-reviewed articles. A PRISMA-compliant search was conducted using multiple databases. Analysis of the ICH pipeline predominantly uses CT imaging and is primarily centered on a classification task. The main focus is on hemorrhage identification, subtype classification, hematoma expansion prediction, and forecasting associated clinical outcomes. The AIS pipeline is primarily based on quantification and therefore uses a variety of imaging techniques to optimize and automate the analysis of a specific set of clinical questions related to the stroke. Core tasks include segmentation of the infarct area, assessment scoring, large vessel occlusion, core-penumbra mismatch analysis, and prediction of outcomes. Convergence is also observed in outcome prediction approaches across both domains. Existing models demonstrate clinically acceptable performance across numerous tasks. Clinical deployment nonetheless remains limited by the lack of external validation, high costs of annotation, demands of real-time processing, and poor prospective evidence. This review offers practical guidance to develop fully operational AI systems that can be integrated into emergency stroke care.

title: Prospective Observational Cohort Study for Predicting Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysm Rupture Risk Using Blood Pressure Variability and 3D Structural Evolution

The study aims to build a time-series dataset combining blood pressure variability (BPV) and three-dimensional (3D) aneurysm morphological evolution, and to develop deep-learning models using long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer networks to predict aneurysm rupture risk. A secondary aim is to compare the new models with traditional scores such as PHASES and to explore how BPV relates to 3D aneurysm change.Participants aged 18-80 years with UIA confirmed by CTA, MRA, or DSA and judged suitable for conservative follow-up will be enrolled consecutively at the study site. Those with imaging contraindications, other major cerebrovascular diseases such as moyamoya or arteriovenous malformation, or severe organ dysfunction are excluded. No study-driven intervention is imposed; routine clinical care continues. Baseline data include demographics, hypertension history, laboratory tests, 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure, home blood pressure for 7 days, optional wearable monitoring, and CTA/MRA/DSA for 3D aneurysm parameters such as volume, surface area, compactness, and sphericity. BPV is summarized using standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and variability independent of the mean.Participants scheduled for in-hospital visits provide written informed consent and are followed at 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96, and 120 months with repeated BPV measurement and imaging. title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support
desc: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

title: ScienceRSI: Recursive Scientific Self-Improvement
desc: Scientific AI can improve cumulatively when capabilities developed in one model become useful learning signals for the next. We introduce ScienceRSI, a framework for recursive scientific self-improvement organized around specialize, verify, transfer, and reuse. Compact experts develop complementary scientific capabilities; shared evaluation identifies their useful contributions; a target model integrates those contributions and can serve as the starting point for further specialization. This organization connects reasoning, model scaling, and iteration through reusable scientific capabilities. We evaluate its transfer step in 4B[->]4B, 4B[->]8B, and 8B[->]27B configurations. ScienceRSI ranks first among the compared methods on all five science benchmarks for the 4B and 8B students. Relative to rubric-based reinforcement learning, scientific-reasoning averages improve by 2.0 and 1.9 percentage points, and domain-science averages by 3.3 and 2.1 points, respectively. In a separate cross-generation 27B extension, reported scores improve over Vanilla on all seven benchmarks, with the unweighted mean rising from 87.3% to 94.0%. These results support verified capability transfer across model scales as a practical foundation for ScienceRSI. Accumulating these gains over repeated rounds is the next step toward sustained recursive scientific improvement.

title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
desc: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's k, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (k range; range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
desc: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

title: AI-Guided Multi-Electrode Transcutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation for Gait Rehabilitation in People With Spinal Cord Injury or Stroke
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Sao Paulo General Hospital; conditions: Spinal Cord Injuries (SCI); type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 24; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] The goal of this clinical trial is to investigate whether personalized multi-electrode transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), guided by machine learning (ML) and combined with gait training, can improve walking function in people with spinal cord injury or stroke compared with single-electrode tonic stimulation combined with the same training. tSCS is a non-invasive technique that delivers electrical pulses through electrodes placed on the skin over the spine to modulate spinal neural circuits, facilitate the recruitment of lower-limb muscles, and support the recovery of voluntary movements. Conventional tSCS typically uses a single stimulation electrode, which may limit selective recruitment of different muscle groups. This study investigates a personalized multi-electrode approach to selectively recruit specific lower-limb muscle groups and deliver stimulation at appropriate phases of the gait cycle, with the aim of improving walking function. The main questions this study aims to answer are: 1. How do electrode positions and stimulation intensities affect selective muscle recruitment, and how do responses vary between participants and days? 2. Can ML-based optimization identify stimulation settings with selectivity comparable to complete mapping of muscle responses, using fewer tests and less time? 3. Does personalized multi-electrode stimulation, synchronized with specific gait phases, improve walking function more than single-electrode tonic stimulation when both are combined with gait training? The study includes 24 participants (14 with spinal cord injury and 10 with stroke) and consists of two stages. Stage 1 - Characterization of tSCS Selectivity and Stimulation Optimization All participants complete two experimental sessions while lying down. Researchers compare muscle responses to stimulation at a central electrode and at multiple spinal electrode locations. Electrical responses in the leg muscles are recorded using surface electromyography (EMG), and spinal reflexes are assessed using paired electrical pulses. By systematically testing electrode positions and stimulation intensities, researchers build a map of which leg muscles respond to each setting (stimulation landscape). They assess the selective recruitment of different muscle groups, compare stimulation locations, and examine differences between participants and across the two sessions. title: Are We Done with UMLS Injection into Language Models for Medical Question Answering?
desc: Maybe not. The Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) has become an oracle for millions of clinicians and health system developers worldwide. Researchers have increasingly used knowledge graphs derived from UMLS to enhance language models' factual accuracy and reasoning traceability in high-stakes tasks. Medical Question Answering (MQA) is a prime testbed for integration, with benchmarks usually involving professional exercises such as disease diagnosis and drug prescription from patient history. Despite the assumed benefits, empirical evidence shows that UMLS-based graph injection typically yields modest performance gains. This paper reviews existing MQA work, critically analyzing the selected UMLS sources and their usage with language models, and probes each of these choices in isolation. We uncover methodological issues never discussed in prior work, from low UMLS coverage to weak subgraph retrieval pipelines. Based on our findings, we provide actionable recommendations to unlock the untapped potential of UMLS as an external knowledge source.

desc: [Briefings in bioinformatics] Bulk T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing enables scalable immune repertoire profiling but does not measure the transcriptional states required to infer T cell functional programs. Paired single-cell RNA/TCR sequencing offers a single-cell functional prior by jointly observing TCR identity and transcriptomic states. However, transferring this prior to bulk repertoires is challenging: sparse and noisy single-cell profiles can distort the functional reference, and the probabilistic relationship between TCR identity and transcriptome-inferred functional state makes direct cell-level alignment unstable, potentially biasing repertoire-level functional composition estimation. We present scMAC, a single-cell-guided framework for functional context completion that infers TCR functional representations reflecting transcriptome-derived T-cell states. scMAC builds a denoised functional reference by integrating multi-scale expression modeling with gene-semantic priors derived from large language model encodings of gene and protein descriptions, improving gene-level functional coherence. It then learns a prototype-guided TCR-to-function mapping that combines paired cell-level latent alignment with functional prototype regularization, enabling robust repertoire-level functional composition estimation. Across real single-cell and paired RNA/TCR datasets, scMAC outperformed existing single-cell representation methods in fine-grained cell-state representation, gene functional consistency, expression recovery, and disease-relevant pathway analysis, achieving an adjusted Rand index of 0.656 on a colorectal cancer dataset with 83 cell subtypes. For repertoire-level functional composition estimation, scMAC closely matched single-cell-derived functional proportions, with an R2 of 0.979 and a Bray-Curtis distance of 0.075. These results support scMAC as a practical route for transferring single-cell-derived functional knowledge to bulk TCR repertoire analysis beyond clonotype identity and clonal abundance. scMAC is publicly available at https://github.com/Bioinformatics7181/scMAC.

title: Effects of AI-Generated Resistance Training on Neuromuscular Performance in Sedentary Men
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Marmara University; conditions: Physical Performance; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 30; status: COMPLETED] The goal of this clinical trial is to learn how an artificial intelligence-generated resistance training program affects muscle performance in sedentary men aged 18 to 35 years. The main questions it aims to answer are: * How does an artificial intelligence-generated resistance training program affect the participants' ability to produce force? * How does this program compare with a resistance training program designed by a professional coach and with no structured resistance training? Researchers will compare three groups: an artificial intelligence-generated resistance training group, a coach-designed resistance training group, and a non-exercising control group. Participants in the two training groups will complete supervised resistance training three times per week for eight weeks. Participants in the control group will not take part in structured resistance training. Researchers will measure muscle performance before and after the eight-week study period to compare changes among the three groups.

title: Energy Efficient Lung Tumor Segmentation with a modified CBAM ENet Skip Model
desc: Lung tumor segmentation plays a vital role in early detection and treatment planning of lung cancer. Although state-of-the-art deep learning models achieve high dice score coefficients (DSC), each forward pass requires computing large amounts of floating point operations, making them computationally expensive, requiring GPU acceleration, and having slow inference speed, limiting real-world clinical deployment. We propose a lightweight, energy-efficient model that leverages the ENet architecture for its real-time inference capability and low computational cost, enhanced with UNet-style skip connections between encoder and decoder stages for feature reuse and the lightweight Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for improved feature representation. The model is trained on publicly available data from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) via the Medical Segmentation Decathlon Challenge (MSD) and evaluated on the Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) dataset. Our model achieves a DSC of 0.90812 (threshold of 0.5) with its compact architecture of 430,052 parameters and 0.549 Giga Multiply-Accumulate operations (GMAC), making it up to 10 times faster, requires 79 times less GMAC than UNet, and has 22 times fewer parameters than SegNet. These characteristics make it well-suited for deployment in clinical settings where computational resources are limited and decrease the cost of utilizing such a system. Additionally, the explainable AI technique of Grad-CAM is used to provide visual interpretability of the model's predictions and to identify regions where segmentation performance requires improvement.
